utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to be everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I'd like to briefly deal with a matter before the witness enters the courtroom, but I'll do that only after I put on the record that the Chamber received a waiver signed by Mr. Mladic to be absent today during the court hearing. We'll therefore proceed in his absence. The other issue I'd like to deal with is that -- it's a remaining issue from the testimony of Mr. Savo Sokanovic. During his testimony on the 18th of May, D1050a was marked for identification pending the English translation. On the 21st of May, the Defence e-mailed the Chamber and the Prosecution, advising that the translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 1D22-4835. On the same day the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence advising that it has no objection to the translation, and the Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to attach the translation, for which I just gave the doc ID, to attach the translation to D1058 and admits D1058 into evidence. The witness may enter the courtroom. Mr. Weber, I don't know whether Madam Usher can hear me when I say that the witness may enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday when we left off I mentioned that there might be one matter that the Prosecution would seek to address with this witness, and we will seek to address it with the witness. I will still endeavour to try to complete in the two-hour range but it may go slightly over and I just wanted to enlighten the Chamber to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Try to do your best, Mr. Weber, and we'll sit the usually one hour and a half sessions today through such sessions. Good morning, Mr. Simic. Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Weber will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P4440 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Simic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Coming up is a document that you saw in the Karadzic case. It is a 19 July 1995 SRK command ammunition expenditure warning from General Milosevic. The first sentence of this warning states: "For more than a month now, with brief interruptions, the enemy has conducted a fierce offensive against our positions with the massive use of artillery, which has not been the case so far." It had not been the case that the ABiH forces prior to June 1995 conducted massive uses of artillery against your forces; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sorry, sir --

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- artillery was supported by --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, just to cut you off, I'm sorry. I'm going to be very short on time today. I asked you a question. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as for then, that offensive, there had not been such strikes like then, mid-June, when the offensive started, and further on. As pointed out here, with interruptions ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, you've answered the question. Let's go through it. The second paragraph begins: "By discussing" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I have to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, what did you intend to say when you say that there had not been such strikes; during that period in mid-1995, or was that during the whole of the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wished to say that as for this period, mid-1995, the middle of June, when the Muslim offensive started, in order to carry out this breakthrough from Sarajevo, there had not been such artillery attacks, such fierce artillery attacks until then. Not as fierce as those that were carried out then. What I tried to say was that this strong artillery activity was expressed because at the same time NATO Rapid Deployment Forces acted against Serb positions in Igman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question. When you said that for that period, the middle of June, there had not been such artillery attacks, such fierce attacks, did you intend to say that such fierce attacks had not happened during those months, or did you want to say that such fierce attacks did not happen, well, let's say on from 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Attacks of such intensity, perhaps from June 1992. They were very intensive then but not as intensive as then in 1995 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you've answered my question. Mr. Weber, I do understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you're under some time restraints, but the witness at least should have an opportunity to give an answer which is clear enough for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours. I also appreciate your sentiments too on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The second paragraph begins by discussing the difficulties of the production of ammunition and the behaviour of the SRK. In the middle of the paragraph, General Milosevic states: "That is why we very often fire at inhabited settlements and specific buildings when there are no combat actions whatsoever, spend vast quantities of ammunition, without paying attention to the fact that we will not have anything to stop the enemy when it comes to mounting a decisive defence." Then in the third paragraph, General Milosevic states: "It is inexplicable that some brigades spend much less ammunition in repelling three or more fierce attacks during the day than others that fire at inhabited settlements when there are no combat actions." First, could you just please tell us the brigades that were firing artillery at inhabited settlements while there were no combat actions?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything to you with certainty. The warning was addressed to all brigades in order to decrease the expenditure of ammunition in view of the enemy offensive and not knowing when it will stop or when we will stop it. As for which brigades carried out such attacks against inhabited areas, I cannot tell you exactly. At the time, I was at the forward command post --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, there are too many microphones on at the same time when the witness is speaking. We have great difficulty following.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Everyone is urged to switch off his microphone to the extent possible. Witness, I think you've answered the question. You don't know which brigades were meant in this text. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, yesterday, when we were looking at some similar information from your immediate superior, at transcript page 35999, when asked about the old habits of units using massive and unselective amounts of artillery, you stated: "If the reference here is to old habits, it's probably the initial period of the war. There were some units that used artillery more than necessary." Who did you have on your mind? What units?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I primarily mean units before brigade artillery groups were established. Time was needed to have this organised, to have units manned. And while they were under the direct command of battalion commanders, probably there were greater use of ammunition then and firing without a particular objective as far as individuals were concerned. And that is the warning. I mean, before brigade artillery groups were established.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you should switch off your microphone during the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thanks, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You can't give the name of any unit?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said according to battalions. They were under the responsibility of battalion commanders. I cannot say which ones specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What brigades -- I mean, there are only so many brigades in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. What brigades were these battalions a part of?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every brigade has battalions within its composition, and you know what the disposition of brigades was and you know what the situation was in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and also on the south-west, on the north, north-west. One knows full well which brigades held positions around Sarajevo. If necessary, I can enumerate all of that for you. But anyway, these are well known things and these are those brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. So you can't name a single brigade which had a battalion that was doing this? Is that what the answer is that you're giving?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say concretely the name of a single battalion or brigade because I do not have such information available, and probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've answered the question. You don't know it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you were in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps throughout the entire war. You attended regular meetings at both the brigade and SRK command level. You sent reports, you received reports, you gave artillery orders, you were directly subordinated to both Generals Galic and General Milosevic. General Milosevic at the same time your immediate superior also sent similar information saying that "we very often fire at inhabited settlements," and he's referring to brigades sometimes doing this. I put it to you that it's not credible that you are saying that you have no idea what brigades General Milosevic is describing in this document.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I did not attend regular meetings of the corps command, because I had my superior, the chief of artillery. He attended those meetings. So only exceptionally a forward command post outside Sarajevo, that is to say Vogosca, Nisici, Trnovo, those command posts. That is where I attended such meetings from time to time and the corps command as well, because I had a chief of artillery who attended these meetings. And in the brigade I attended meetings when it was necessary for the chiefs of arms and services to attend, to present their proposals, to say what the problems were and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This document was sent through the chain of the command, and we see that your immediate superior knows similar information. Are you really saying that you weren't aware of this same information?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could just conclude from this order that there had been such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that you're minimising what this document says, based on the scope of the conduct that's described by General Milosevic. Do you have any other comments?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I am saying here everything that I know and everything that I remember from the period of war when I held certain positions as recorded in my statement. I have no reason to keep silent about anything. I have no reason to conceal anything, and I am going to speak here to the best of my knowledge about that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph, which starts with the statement: "While we use massive artillery at a time when the enemy had a just a few mortars and the occasional gun, we did not manage to settle the war ..." And then it continues. You acknowledge that that's the case, right? That's what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acknowledge that Muslim forces had less artillery pieces and artillery units in the initial period of the war, less than the Sarajevo Romanija Corps that held positions around Sarajevo. However, during the course of the war, this balance was struck, a balance was struck. So in 1995, their artillery units, the artillery units of the Muslim forces, were far superior to those on Serb positions around Sarajevo, along with the support of NATO Rapid Deployment Forces and later on NATO airforce as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've again ignored a part of the information in the sentence. The SRK used massive amounts of artillery during that time; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have already said that they had more artillery pieces and more artillery units in that period. So this is an order, a warning about that period, when there was an overspending of ammunition. Perhaps more ammunition was spent than necessary while they were under the command of battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that massive artillery use at those times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, at the beginning of the war, and I've already pointed out that their offensive at the end of May, beginning of June, 1992, was so intensive, and according to the reports of the Muslim forces themselves, they were attempting a breakthrough and we had sustained great losses on account of that, what their artillery did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, why don't you answer my question. My question was that at the time when the enemy had just a few mortars and the occasional gun, whether at that time the VRS, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, used massive artillery? That's the simple question. That's written. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree that there were two or three mortars and a cannon or two. This is written figuratively. But it was less --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm asking you now for the third time whether at that time whether massive artillery was used by your forces, as written in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not say there was massive, but they used artillery more than usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to item 4 of the warning, General Milosevic orders: "In order to achieve a surprise effect and inflict the highest enemy losses, produce strong planned concentrated fire from several weapons from different directions at a specific time, instead of firing one or two weapons for an hour at the same target." As we see here, it is possible to produce concentrated fire from several weapons that are located at different locations; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, possibly. If firing positions allow for that possibility. So there was that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 32 of your statement, you indicate that you are aware of information regarding the Markale II shelling, which is after this order. That there were five rounds fired from two different directions. This is the type of firing that is consistent with the instruction that we see here; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. The type of firing that is consistent with the instruction? Which instruction? You mean the concentration of fire-power, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, according to your statement in paragraph 32, you're aware that there was four rounds fired from 240 degrees, I believe is what you say, that landed in the vicinity of the down-town area and that there was another round from 170 degrees that hit the area of the market-place. That's consistent with this type of order; right? Concentrated firing from two different directions.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this has nothing whatsoever to do with that order and that this doesn't to pertain that at all. It has nothing whatsoever to do with concentration of fire-power and several objectives. It really has nothing to do with any of that. That really is my assumption. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In item 5 General Milosevic orders the commander of the Ilijas Brigade to prevent artillery fire on settlements and positions of the Kiseljak HVO because of agreements on mutual co-operation. He does not order the other brigades to prevent artillery fire on Muslim settlements as part of this warning; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the order, it seems that the order was only issued to the Ilijas Brigade, but through the order we can see that he is warning all units not to spend ammunition unnecessarily. So from this paragraph, I see that the order was issued to the Ilijas Brigade only.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32621 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This morning I'm going to try to get through a number of sequence of events with you. This is a 14 September 1992 SRK command combat order, which was issued at 1000 hours. It is General Galic's operational order number 1. In the first part of the order, General Galic discusses Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have the next page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under item 4.1, there are tasks for the Ilidza and Igman Brigades to carry out an attack toward areas in the western part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And then I believe this is in the next page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of the section, one of the brigades that is listed as part of the support forces is the 1st Smbr. The 1st Smbr provided fire support for this attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where there was a possibility not only in the context of this attack but whenever there was a possibility for the 1st Sarajevo Brigade to provide support to other units, it was done. Support was lent to the Ilidza Brigade, the Igman Brigade, the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade or any other. Support was lent whenever there was this possibility. I don't remember this specific case. If there is an engagement plan, perhaps that could jog my memory. But it is probable. One needs to bear in mind the position of the firing positions of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, what were the targets, and whether there was this possibility to target them. Such a possibility did exist in the area of Igman and in the Ilidza Brigade and we lent support to those units throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this document into evidence. I am then going to call up another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32621 receives number P7408.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32622 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Witness, could I again urge you to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is an excerpt from annex 6 of the 1994 final report of the United Nations commission of experts, which was established pursuant to a Security Council Resolution, number 780. This specific part relates to the day of 14 September 1992. According to information from three news sources, the targets hit on this day included the old town, the city centre, the area near the Holiday Inn, the school-yard at the children's embassy, an apartment bloc north of the river, Marin Dvor, and it mentions the parliament building, government headquarters, and two fire-gutted office towers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The narrative events for this day states: "Thousands of residents strolling to work and outside their homes, enjoying sunshine were caught by intense day long salvos of tank, cannon, mortar, and rocket fire, some of which set blazes in homes less than 200 metres from the UN headquarters. The attacks began at around 10.00 a.m. At least 20 people were reported killed and 60 wounded in two hours." This attack appears to have began shortly after the 1000 hour order from General Galic that same day. This is how General Galic's order was implemented. That's what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood well, this was September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah, you understand it well. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders of superior commands were implemented to the letter. When Muslim forces skillfully provoked attacks on their firing positions close to these facilities mentioned in the document, that is when we considered the truce to have been violated and instances of disobeying orders occurred. General Milosevic and other officers were informed of it, and such fire needed to be responded to. I don't think anyone would have opened fire at these targets had it not been for the fire coming from their vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you your answer makes no sense. This was a massive attack that lasted for multiple hours throughout many different parts of the city at or near shortly after the time General Galic issued an order. That's what's happened. And I'll give you one last opportunity to make any other comments you want to make.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for some things taking place immediately after the order was issued, that does not mean that the attacks had not been provoked. This is a result of the Muslim propaganda coming through their media. They used it very skillfully. They would open fire and then target civilian facilities. They did so countless times during the war. I have no other answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I appreciate you don't want to answer the question. Just let me ask you something for factually specific: Did your observers see the houses on fire that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought I should wait, but this comment is unfair, saying that the witness would not answer. He did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You invited the witness to comment, Mr. Weber. That's what he did. And whether you like the comment or not is a different matter. So it's not an objection, but could you refrain from unnecessarily making statements like you did. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did your observers see the houses on fire that day? They must have; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have in mind my observers from my unit or UNPROFOR observers?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I said "your observers," meaning your -- the observers that are associated with your brigade.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My observers must have seen it because they were at their observation locations. However, before that they probably had asked that fire be open at certain enemy targets which placed Serb forces in danger in depth of our territory in Lukavica and further afield or from the other side of north-north-west. So they must have seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are entering the area of conclusions rather than factual knowledge. Tell us what you know, tell us what you remember, and otherwise tell us that you don't know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders the document into evidence at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32622 receives number P7409.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7409 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P463 for the witness. P463, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 6 October 1992 SRK command order for the next combat operation from General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this page under section 4, we see that General Galic decides to engage in a decisive defence of many positions leading out of Sarajevo from the north and the south and keep a firm blockade of the city. In the next paragraph, he refers to offensive operations to take possession of the wider area of Trnovo and establish a corridor with the Herzegovina Corps. He then orders these offensive/defensive operations to be carried out in three stages lasting from 30 to 45 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 10 of the B/C/S original and page 7 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you were reading the offensive/defensive operations in the plural. The text itself is only in singular.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under section 6.2 of this order, General Galic indicates artillery support will be provided by the Corps artillery group, KAG, from the strength of the 4th MAP. In conjunction with this type of order, operational order, the SRK command would then issue tasking orders for the use were artillery during these operations; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 464. 464. P464. Or I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'd said the wrong thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it is a 65 ter or is it a P number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I misspoke. Exhibit P464. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is an 11 October 1992 SRK command order from Radislav Cvetkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And it is Exhibit P464 and not like the number given in page 18, line 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This order relates to the support that the 4th MAP and the 4th MAOAP are supposed to provide.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions. And I will be focusing on section (c).

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In section (c) of this order we see a number of firing tasks. Mid-way in the section, it is ordered: "Support the offensive combat operations by opening fire along the following axes ..." And then there are three axes that are provided. Just to take the first one as an example, it states: Faletici-Zmajevac. This is an instruction for firing positions from Faletici to fire into the area of Zmajevac; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The last one indicates that there should be fire from Borija into Bascarsija; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's the third one in the section that says: "Support the offensive combat Operations by opening fire along the following axes ..." There are three axes then provided, Faletici-Zmajevac, Mrkovici-Breka and the third one Borija to Bascarsija. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: None of these targeted areas are near Trnovo. They're all within the area the SRK referred to as the inner ring; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is discussed here is lending support to our forces along these axes, as it says Faletici-Zmajevac, Mrkovici-Breka, Borija-Bascarsija. That is an axis. Our position was at Faletici, it was in the direction of Zmajevac, our position at Mrkovici in the direction of Breka. So support our forces from that axis, be on the ready. But it doesn't mean to engage, necessarily. It just means to be prepared to counter their attack or any other activity because their forces had to be tied down in other parts of the Sarajevo even though attacks may not have been directed at Trnovo directly from those areas. That is precisely why all corps units were included in this order. We could not rely only on lending support along the attack axis but it means lending support to all those who are specified therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We see that it says to support offensive combat operations and we've seen General Galic describe what those offensive combat operations were at the time. My question to you is just really simple: None of these things are in the area of Trnovo; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving you a simple answer. Does it not mean that support is lent to those forces if their forces are tied down at a different front line and then such forces cannot be used along an axis we have foreseen as the attack axis? Support is not only given along attack axes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I ask you: You again and again stress that it was to return fire, whereas the document says opening fire. Opening fire is something you start. That's at least my understanding of the word "opening." It doesn't say support the offensive combat operation but don't forget to return any fire if it comes from one of these axis. It says support the offensive combat by opening fire at certain axis. That's what we'd like to better understand how what you say and what is written here, how that can be reconciled or whether -- to explain how the one is consistent with the other in view of the language used.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can have an explanation for your description of the English language saying "opening fire" is the first party firing? I'm confused by that because it's contrary to my understanding of English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I didn't think, Mr. Ivetic, that you were the one who was examining this witness. But apart from that, I'll not be formal on that. Opening fire, in my view, is not the same as returning fire. That's what I wanted to express.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I would respectfully reflect that that is not my understanding of the English language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- okay. Then I will ask any native speaker to address the matter so as to better understand as a non-native speaking person the language which is used. I'm always open for that. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, since B/C/S is my mother tongue. In the document, not "opening fire" is referred to but "executing fire."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then the native speakers will find out whether that's different or not. I'll leave it to that. You've pointed at what you consider to be possibly a imprecision, inaccuracy in the translation of this document. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution have 65 ter 10973 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if the document can be released in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I might have to return to that. Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P430 for the witness. Thank you so much for the Chamber's indulgence. I am going to go to Exhibit P561, before moving on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is an UNPROFOR incident report before you from the date of 1 November 1992. The events described are within the 30 to 40 days after General Galic's order from 6 October. The report states: "At 1000 hours on 31 October 1992 a major mortar and artillery attack started on the centre of the city of Sarajevo. The first few rounds caught many civilians in the open, thus causing casualties." The second paragraph starts: "We were presented with three casualties, all with varying degrees of shrapnel wounds." The report then mentions two additional casualties and states: "Of these additional two, one was a man of about 60 years who had a bad leg wound and possible injury caused by shrapnel hole (small) in his side." This document then describes additional firing that was going on as they were trying to treat this individual and indicates the hospitals were full. These casualties were the result of the orders we just looked at. That's what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These events did occur after the order as stated in the report. At the firing positions of my brigade, there were UNPROFOR officers round-the-clock with an interpreter. They noted any opening of fire from the position in terms of what units opened fire, how many rounds, and at what target, as well as for what reasons the fire was opened. So they knew. They had that information. If you had information that would confirm it was done by my unit, I am prepared to answer any questions. But I do know it was not the case. It was in the period that I was the chief of artillery and commanded the artillery regiment. I was familiar with almost each and every instance of opening fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P430 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is another SRK command operational order. This one's dated 26 November 1992, for further activities. It's also from General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of the B/C/S and page 5 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, could I seek clarification. You earlier said: "If you have information that would confirm it was done by my unit, I am prepared to answer any questions." And then you say that was not the case. And two lines later, you say: "I was familiar with almost each and every instance of opening fire." Did you mean instances of opening fire by your unit or more broadly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had my unit in mind. The brigade artillery crew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under section 4 of this order, General Galic decides: "The main forces of the Corps should continue to protect the lines and positions reached through persistent and active defence, whereas the rest of the forces should start offensive operations with the aim of keeping the Sarajevo and Igman sectors under complete blockade, and depending on the development of the situation tighten the circle around the city;" He then states: "... following thorough preparations and after receiving special approval from the Corps Command, cut off and isolate specific parts of the city and the surrounding settlements;" These were the objectives of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the tasks contained in the order to conduct operations in the direction of Trnovo. It also refers to some other forces and the main axis was the one in the direction of Trnovo. The other forces had to be used to maintain the blockade and try and carry out incursions, but that did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On the next page, General Galic orders these operations to last for a period of 30 to 40 days starting on 2 December 1992. The Smbr is one of the brigades we see in this order assigned tasks pursuant to this operation, along with the rest of the SRK units, much like the last operational order we looked at. Your brigade took part in these operations to keep Sarajevo under blockade; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brigade had positions right around Sarajevo; that is to say, from the railway 1in the direction of Trebevic. My unit held positions and certainly took part in the defence of Serb positions, Serb territory in that zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P4423 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is another SRK artillery order from Colonel Cvetkovic to the 4th MAP and the 4th MAOAP. This one is the same date as the operational order that we just looked at, the 26th of November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You were referring to 4th MAOAP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: MP -- excuse me, it was the document. I might have mispronounced. I was referring to the mixed anti-armour regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: MP --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: MPOAP. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this page, again under section (c), we see the firing tasks that were ordered. The firing tasks are almost identical to the one that we saw for the previous month. Again, the order states: "Support the offensive by engaging in fire along the following axes ..." And the exact same axes are listed as in the October order. These are the same firing tasks that we saw previously; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but do read the first paragraph here where it says: "Prevent enemy attack ..." All of these are tasks of the artillery. From Sarajevo, firing at such and such areas. Then support the counterattack of our forces. If their attack is successful, then we should launch a counterattack in the following areas and only then support offensive activities. And we've already said that a moment ago, by firing at Faletici-Zmajevac, Mrkovici-Breka, Borija-Bascarsija. Do allow me to say this too: In artillery, firing is planned for support, for engaging a target that is closer or further away. If we are attacking, it doesn't mean that that fire is actually going to take place. Always a lot more is planned than actually carried out. Maybe there will be no firing at all depending on how combat evolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence, and as an example I'd be referring to the Chamber to Exhibit P425, that the pattern of shelling during the month of December 1992 was widely dispersed throughout the city. The fact is these orders were executed and areas all over the city of Sarajevo were shelled throughout December 1992. That's what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order of the corps command was to shell the entire city in December 1992? I don't know of that order, to carry out shelling of the city. I really don't know about this. And the corps never issued such orders. They issued orders to fire at their targets if they were within the area of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, we can see that there's areas all over the city that are mentioned in these orders. What I'm saying is these orders were carried out and there was shelling that was widely dispersed throughout the city in December 1992. That's what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order envisages fire and it orders the preparation of fire. And as I explained a moment ago, artillery prepares this fire. Now, whether they will be carried out, that I don't know. It all depends on the situation on the ground, on the combat operations involved, on the tempo involved, and so on and so forth; that is to say, the concrete situation. And sometimes none of what is planned is actually carried out. That is the essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us whether what was planned was carried out in relation to this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this order, I know that the main objective was not reached that; that is to say, the area of Trnovo was not taken. And that was the main objective, to take Trnovo, and that was not carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, we are talking about artillery tasks. Not about the end result of the operation. Could you tell us -- where you said several times that artillery support would not necessarily mean that fire was opened, could you tell us whether in relation to this order that fire, as planned, was opened? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say with any degree of certainty whether everything was carried out or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32620 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 5 March 1993 Sarajevo Romanija Corps command tasking order from General Galic, which was sent to all brigades and regiments. The first paragraph refers to the completed analysis of combat readiness for the SRK in 1992 and an assessment by VRS Main Staff team of SRK units. The first section relates to command and control. Under task 1 of the order, General Galic states: "Carry out the tasks from Directives nos. 2, 3 and 4 of the GSV RS so that the planning and carrying out of operations from Directive no. 5 may be initiated on time." In March 1993 the Sarajevo Romanija Corps was still carrying out tasks from the Main Staff directives nos. 2, 3, and 4; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what these directives pertain to so I cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, Directive 5 that's mentioned here is in evidence before this Chamber and relates to Operation Lukavac 93, which you comment on in your statement. The SRK was preparing for Operation Lukavac 93 months in advance, correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for the explanation. Now I know that it is Directive 5. I didn't know. I'd forgotten. Yes, my brigade was preparing, as the artillery was, for Lukavac 1993 and my brigade took part in it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under number 5, General Galic states: "The entire process of preparation, organisation and carrying out combat activities should be based on offensive and active activities with the application of defence only as the last resort ..." Colonel Simic, the fact is the SRK's entire process of planning, organisation, and preparation, and even carrying out activities was based on offensive operations. That's the truth, what we see here in your own corps commander's order; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. As for offensive activities, I would single out this operation that I mentioned in my statement, Lukavac 93. And the offensive activities of improving the tactical positions around Sarajevo that we discussed yesterday in the area of Brajkovac, Vrakusa. That is to say that there were other parts of the front as well. The improvement of positions, taking of Grdonj and so on. As for this order where it says carry out offensives, well, that means that infantry units, infantry battalions at positions should fire from infantry weapons all the time. And as for support, if they asked their brigade artillery groups for that kind of support, they would get it. But masking preparation towards Trnovo for Lukavac 1993, that is my opinion, so that they would think that a breakthrough, the take-over of Sarajevo was being planned, which was not actually the idea, so I think that that might be the underlying idea of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, throughout your testimony and yesterday and today, you've been claiming and making various justifications that you were acting in defence and just returning fire. Actually, according to this -- and now you're not acknowledging, I think, that the full scope of what this says and what General Galic is saying, that the entire process of preparation, organisation, and carrying out combat activities should be based on offensive and active activities. You're not being forthcoming. That's what you're doing; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am telling the truth totally, and I am speaking in all sincerity. And there is no reason for me to make any kind of excuses by way of saying that I was only carrying out defensive activity. This order, that is Lukavac 1993, that is that operation has to do with that order. I am saying that that is the only offensive activity carried out by the Sarajevo Romanija Corps in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32620 receives number P7410.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7410 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this Trial Chamber has also received additional operational orders from the SRK command throughout the war, including General Galic's operational order for Lukavac 93 which orders a 155-millimetre howitzer battery to "prevent to lift the blockade of Sarajevo by firing on the sectors of the Stari Grad municipality." This is Exhibit P6549. They've also received the SRK operational order from January 1994 which orders the use of all available means to penetrate areas like Dobrinja. This is just weeks before civilians were killed and wounded in a humanitarian line in this area. The same orders task firing into the region of Alipasino Polje just four days after six children were killed while sledding in the snow and supporting offensive activities from firing from areas -- from firing positions in Mrkovici just two weeks before the Markale I shelling. For the record, I'm referring to P4476. What I'm saying to you, sir, is that we've looked at some operational orders. The SRK continued to engage in operations of an offensive nature and shelled various areas of the city throughout the entire war; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give any other answer besides the one I've given. As for offensive activities, the ones that I know about, those are the ones I've already told you about. That we would cut off the city, that we would do something -- I mean, from the beginning of the war the combat positions did not change. There were lesser or greater minor changes, from the beginning of the war. Which shows that there were no offensive activities. And also, there was no plan to relocate the artillery forward for a further task and so on and so forth. So maybe these are offensive actions around Sarajevo. No way are these offensive operations. We kept defending our defensive positions, and that's what the enemy said themselves, in order to protect the ethnic areas of the Serb population behind enemy lines, deep in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P3, page 80 in e-court. And I'm just going to try to get some marking done on a map before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if it comes to marking of maps on the screen, would you carefully wait until you're instructed to mark something and then follow the instructions as how to mark it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could wait until I actually ask you to mark something. But just so we know, you are familiar with the area that's depicted in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 of your statement, you list part of the combat disposition of the 1st Smbr. You state that the command post of the mixed artillery division of the brigade was in the Uzdojnice village sector. Could you please mark the command post of this artillery division with the letters KM.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you mark it with the position -- with the letters KM?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You mentioned one 120-millimetre mortar battery in the Uzdojnice village sector. Could you please mark the location of this battery on the map with the letters MB.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Next you reference a firing position of the 128-millimetre Plamen multiple rocket launchers, VBRs, in the area of the Uzdojnice village. Can you please mark this firing position with the letters VBR?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You refer to one 120-millimetre mortar battery in the Kraljevo Brdjo sector. Could you please mark this location with the letters MB.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we have twice MB.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I know. I'm just using it for "mortar battery."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful if we could distinguish between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should we mark it as 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That would be great. That was what I was going to be suggesting. Could you mark the one in the Uzdojnice area as MB1 and the one you marked if the Kraljevo Brdjo area as MB2?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You also referred to a 120-millimetre D30 howitzer battery firing position in the Tilava village. Could you please mark this location with the letter H.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Chamber has received evidence in this case about the address of Toplika Cesta 57R in the area of Toplik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'm referring to P537, page 60 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you see the road of Toplika Cesta on this map?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The evidence that the Chamber has received is that this is the address of the UNMO Lima 5 observation post. Can you please mark the approximate location of Toplika Cesta 57R on this map with the letters L5?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They changed locations there. I remember two or three locations. Now, I don't know. I mean, perhaps I could with some approximation. One was closer to this Toplik, towards the west of this howitzer position. And before that, it was closer to the command post in Uzdojnice. So they often changed their locations. They were always on duty at the command post, 24 hours a day. So I don't know where I should mark this. At one or the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm asking -- the Chamber has received evidence that their observation post was -- we can talk about it further, but we've received evidence that the observation post was at the address of Toplika Cesta 57R. Are you able to indicate approximately where that was along the road of Toplika Cesta in Toplik?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter L?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: L5, if you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document. I do have more questions on this, but it would be a good time, actually, for the break, if Your Honours wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map as marked will receive number P7411.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. You would like to take the break now, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could. I think that will allow me to probably more efficiently go through this and finish in a more efficient manner after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness already follow the usher and leave the courtroom, but give the usher one second to save the marked document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take that break, as I said I welcome any further clarification of terms like "opening fire" or "returning fire" or "effecting fire" or firing, whatever it is. I think the Chamber could also be assisted if there is any translation issue. And if you would do so, then I would share with you one of the things that makes it difficult for me to have a contextual understanding of these terms. If one gives instructions a few days before something happens and then if the instruction is "open fire," if that would be also would include returning fire, then I'm struggling with the idea that how you could know two days in advance where the fire comes from that you should respond to. That is one of the issues of contextual understanding of this language. Again, if there is any translation issue we would like to know that as well so I have to have the best understanding of the texts and the best understanding of the testimony that is before us. We take a break and will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, any update as to how you reorganised the remainder of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, I think I'm ahead of schedule and I really appreciate, Your Honours, for the break because I think I'll probably finish within a half-hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Stojanovic, your timing is still the same as it was yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a bit longer in order to deal with the issue that was opened before the break concerning some documents and translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm then confident that we would easily conclude also re-examination in this session? Half an hour for Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps quarter of an hour for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that the Chamber then earlier takes a break, that we make that break slightly longer, and that we will deliver quite a number of decisions after that break so that we have a clean slate or an almost clean slate by the end of today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32624 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, there is no current translation for this -- oh, there is. If you could please follow along with me. Colonel Simic, this is a UNMO Sarajevo Lima team operation order, dated 22 October 1993. In paragraph 1 it indicates that UNMO Sarajevo is deployed on both sides of the warring parties. The order then indicates it is the UNMO's task to monitor Serb and Bosnian fire. And under the first item, it says: "Observing preferably by patrolling activities, or through the OP facilities." And then we see it's also part of their responsibilities under item 3 to "monitor gun and mortar positions." The UNMOs were monitoring your positions from their observation post facilities and through patrols; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, we acknowledge that the UNMOs did come at times to your various gun positions and that they did come to your headquarters sometimes more frequent than other times. That was the case; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were constantly at the regiment command post around-the-clock as of late June when UNMOs were introduced until the end of the war. They were constantly at the regimental command post at Breka. They came to the brigade command occasionally. I don't know how frequently. Given the fact that the command post was in the area of the firing positions, they could observe the firing positions through the window of the command facility and they also visited them directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: With respect to the last item, we do acknowledge that, and we've seen you mark where the general area, Lima 5, was in relation to many of your positions. There is a difference that I'm trying to understand here, though. From this observation post you wouldn't consider that they were constantly around the clock at all these positions; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lima 5 was the location where all of the observers were accommodated. It was the house they used. From the house, a duty UNPROFOR officer would go to the observation post where they would be on duty for 24-hours a day, as of late June until the end of the war. They rotated daily. They would come in the morning, spend 24 hours there, then the next person would come and so on and so forth. There was an interpreter there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm not going to spend a significant amount of time with this because the Chamber has received a lot of evidence from UNMOs. You agree that under the organisation of this in part 3, which is on the next page in the B/C/S version, that Lima 5 was based in Toplik; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 32624 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7412.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32625.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I want to now go through an example of a UNMO patrol report. This is a -- I picked this example because it's an UNMO patrol report from Lima 5. It is dated 7 September, 1993. Under number 2, it says: "Mission: Patrol L5A and update gun's serial numbers." Under the significant points, we see the serial numbers for six 120-millimetre mortars and what appears to be six 120-millimetre howitzers. There are also eight-digit grid reference that we checked which appeared to be correspond to the area of Uzdojnice. In September 1993, the Smbr did have six 120-millimetre mortars and six 122-millimetre howitzers in the area of Uzdojnice; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The report lists the names of the mission commander and the other personnel, and then beside number 6 it stays: "Patrol start time: 0900 - end time: 1130." Sir, this document indicates that, in fact, UNMOs were coming to your gun positions sometimes for a period of two, two and a half hours in this instance, to just check on your positions. That's what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened that they occasionally toured the positions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- well, actually, since we're on this document. I see that there is some additional information in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The main direction of the 120-millimetre howitzers appears to be 300 degrees. That would be pointing towards Dobrinje; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Direction: Lukavica, Dobrinje, Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The 122-millimetre howitzer, the main direction I see is 230 degrees. That would be pointing towards roughly the area Sokolovic Kolonija and Hrasnica; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sokolovic Kolonija, Hrasnica, and Igman. That was the axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document receives number P7413.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to have it admitted, you should pause for a second. P7413 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My apologies. Your Honours, that last matter the Prosecution addressed with respect to an outstanding matter that had been left over from a previous witness, Dusan Skrba. If there's any other particular outstanding matters related to that the Prosecution would be happy to provide any additional information. The Chamber had asked for reports concerning the activities of the UNMOs and the firing positions related to the Smbr.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment, nothing comes to our minds. Let's hope that it doesn't change.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P580.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: While this is coming up, you would agree, and it seems from your comments yesterday, that Colonel Tadija Manojlovic was very knowledgeable about artillery; right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that he was chief of artillery of the SRK, yes. Although, I was not competent to assess his professionalism and competency. He was my superior. Someone, whoever appointed him to that position, must have assessed that instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a SRK document dated 26th April 1995 to the VRS Main Staff. It's from Colonel Manojlovic. In paragraph 1, he says: "At the morning briefing of 26.04.1995 the decision was taken to carry out firing using aerial bombs on the village of Donji Kotorac (tunnel entry)." It's then noted. In the second paragraph, the firing is supposed to be executed in the early morning hours and all the necessary preparations for the firing were to be executed beforehand. In paragraph 3, it talks about the assessment of all the facilities and it mentions an observation post with a very specific trigger point and the fact that it was about -- that two UNPROFOR points were almost 200 metres away. In the next paragraph, he additionally says: "Our forward defence line is approximately 500 metres away from the tunnel entrance in the direction of Kula." He then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says: "The direction of fire is over the Kula restaurant."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is over the Kula restaurant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what you said, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So because -- then he goes on to say: "Because I was unable to report this information to the Commander - after the reconnaissance - as he was in the zone of responsibility of the Igman Brigade, I have abandoned the firing on account of jeopardising the security of own forces and that of the UN forces." Here we have Colonel Manojlovic cancelling the firing of or the use of an aerial bomb out of concern that his own forces might be hit who are approximately 500 metres away and UN forces of a lesser distance are also there. The fact is, sir, modified air bombs were -- had at least an imprecision of at least 500 metres; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I would not agree. I am familiar with the impact of air bombs. I could personally observe their flight and I was satisfied with their precision. The measures undertaken by Colonel Manojlovic were taken because UNPROFOR forces were so close. He gave up from targeting because the commander was not present as well. As for the Muslim population in the Kotorac area where the tunnel entrance was, by that point there was no one there any more. There was just the entrance of the tunnel behind a house. And the other point of entry was on the other side at Dobrinje. I believe he made this decision solely due to the fact that the UNPROFOR forces were so close.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, that's not all this document says. Colonel Manojlovic says: "I have abandoned the firing on account of jeopardising the security of own forces and that of the UN forces." So he's not just concerned about the safety of the UN but also his own forces. You see that, right?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he took care of his own forces, but it doesn't only deal with the line at 500 metres distance because the distance varied according to location. It is true that in this report to the Main Staff he pointed that fact out as well as one of the reasons for giving up. As regards precision of aerial bombs, as far as I could observe I was quite satisfied with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain to me what you meant when you said: "It doesn't only deal with the line at 500 metres distance because the distance varied according to location." Distance between what and what varied to the location of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The front end of our forces at some places was indeed 500 metres away from the tunnel, but there were places where the distance was smaller or larger than that. So the distance is not always 500 metres between the tunnel entrance and the front end of our forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if I understand your previous testimony correctly, you believe that there was some precision to the modified aerial bombs because there were rockets attached to them that had stabilisers. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aerial bombs did not have a certain degree of precision. They were as precise as classical assets. They did have a degree of deviation from the desired target, but it all fell within the shooting tables as was the case with the other artillery assets. As for the aerial bombs, we did not mount any rockets on them but we actually turned them into rockets by virtue of mounting a rocket engine on a bomb, that bomb became a rocket. If you attach a rocket engine at the rear of a bomb, it becomes a rocket launched from the ground rather than classical assets that would be dropped from the plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We appreciate that. But is a part of that reasoning that you have, in terms of the precision, the fact that these rocket engines that were attached to the bomb, that they had stabilisers which would stabilise then the projectile in flight?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P4525.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're referring to firing tables. Did you have firing tables for these air bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the two occasions when I was present and observing the activity of those air bombs, since I was at the position where it was mounted on the launching pad, I could observe the tables similar to the ones used by standard assets. Depending on different elements, there were certain requirements that needed to be met to have them fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, they were not produced according to a specific standard, isn't it? It was not factory standardised, controlled production, or was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how they were produced and where in terms of the launching pads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you don't know that. Can you tell us whether any tables you may have seen -- first of all, do you have any further details of the tables you saw; and second, could you tell us whether these tables were produced on the basis of testing of that type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not certain. I suppose that such tables were created based on tests and different parameters were entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't know that, what you assume or what you suppose is a different matter. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Colonel Simic, just based on Judge Orie's questions, I'd just like to confirm something you stated in the Karadzic case. It's a quote that I'm referring to at transcript page 30100. In those proceedings, you stated: "I was not involved in compiling firing tables, so I wouldn't know what they entailed." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't believe that. I don't think I said that I wasn't aware of the contents of the tables. I must have said that I saw the tables and that they contained all the elements that would otherwise be found in the tables for standard assets. I can't specify each and every such element, but the same thing applied to the launchers of aerial bombs. I don't think I said that I didn't know what was in the tables, because I was well aware of it. Perhaps I said that I didn't know where the testing was done and how. I really don't know that. But I do know that firing tables are created based on testing, and I suppose that had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, and I would just for the record, if we could excerpt just the full question and answer from transcript pages 30099 and 30100 and tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know how long that is and we haven't seen it, did we?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I can call it up, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or if you read the relevant portion -- or you could call it up. That's perhaps better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32641. And if we could go to page 64. And I'm going to line 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is during the cross-examination. It was stated to you: "Stop, please. Stop. You don't have to ask rhetorical questions. We can get this straightened" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness cannot read it, so could you please slowly read it for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It was stated to you: "Stop, please. Stop. You don't have to ask rhetorical questions. We can get this straightened out very quickly. It's not the bomb itself that has a firing table because it's normally dropped out of an aeroplane, right; it's the rocket that has a firing table?" Your answer was: "Correct. However, in view of the situation that we discussed just a while ago, we -- I told you how we launched it. It could not just be launched arbitrarily. All the other elements had to be provided in advance in order to launch an air bomb. You had to have firing tables, and those firing tables are made by experts. I was not involved in compiling firing tables so I wouldn't know what they entailed. But just like any other artillery weapons excerpts are familiar with the type of shells, you determine distances for a certain type of ammunition, there are firing tables for every artillery weapon. And that's how things were done for air bombs as well. That was done subsequently when those launchers were crafted, and when the launching of air bombs were started in that way, firing tables were devised. They were compiled, they had to be prepared in advance because everything else would have just been shooting blindly, shooting in the air, I don't know where. Firing tables were compiled in order to hit a target and they accompanied every piece of weaponry, of course." Do you stand by this evidence?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't understand how we see here that I stated I hadn't seen it. It is impossible. I know I said that I did not take part in their creation. And as I said now, I know who was usually tasked with creating firing tables and how they were created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is how your words were recorded. If you say that's not what I said, we'll go back to the audio of that session and we'll find out whether your criticism is justified or whether just your own recollection is not good. We can check the audio, we can check the interpretation of the words you spoke, and we can then check whether this record is accurate, yes or no. If you say that's not what I said, that's what will be done. Do you say that it's not accurately recorded what Mr. Weber read to you a second ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is incorrect. I would actually like to have that listened to. I don't know what the context must have been that I would say I don't know what was in the firing tables. I just said I saw them. I don't know how it was interpreted. If it was interpreted well, we can check that against the recording and verify the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I think what Mr. Weber read to you a minute ago didn't say that you never saw them. So therefore, you are commenting on something Mr. Weber may have said earlier when we had not the text of your testimony before us as recorded. But, Mr. Weber, it may be that if you continue that the problem may be over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah. And, Your Honours, I'm happy to tender whatever section the parties think is necessary to understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But in fairness --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying. What I was trying to go after very quickly was the fact that he was not familiar with the content of whatever tables he claims to have seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But let's have a look at what you put to the witness because this may have created part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful if we continue reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'd also like to check what Mr. Weber put to the witness earlier. Yes, what was earlier put to you by Mr. Weber was: "I was not involved in compiling firing tables, so I wouldn't know what they entailed." That is what Mr. Weber earlier put to you and he now read a part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is exactly what we can see on lines 2 and 3 of this page in front of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say that's not what you said? Then we'll check that. If you had not said "I wouldn't know what they entailed," then we will verify that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I did not say that. How could I have said that? When I saw the tables and when I know what they contain, I mean really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether it's a mistake or not. But you are challenging that you said it and that will be verified. And perhaps, apparently, you are concerned about whether you ever saw them. Perhaps, Mr. Weber, the next few lines might ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And just to be clear, sir, here it is not being said that you didn't know what they contained. It's said that you didn't know what they entailed, which is slightly different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
