utterances.text: Mr. Weber, perhaps the next question and answer might assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course. I'll read it into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Starting on line 14: "Did you ever see one of these firing tables? "A. Yes, on those two occasions -- actually on just one occasion. The first time I saw those firing tables, I saw how elements were calculated and applied to the weapon that was used on the Nisici plateau." Is that correct or do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I stated there, that I saw the firing tables on the basis of which elements were being calculated. It's not that they make it possible to calculate the elements. Not a single table calculates elements. Elements are calculated separately for each and every target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just happy to verify what he said and tender this section of his previous evidence since he's questioning whether he said stuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that that we should admit into evidence, also in view of what happened, these two pages, these extracts. Is it uploaded as such?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will reserve a number for that. Mr. Stojanovic, I think it would be wise to have the transcript verified and the interpretations verified. And if that would give us any reason to revisit the matter, I take it that you'll draw our attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. Because I think that this witness has precisely been saying that in his answers, so let this be verified, listened to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Apparently you have a recollection yourself as well, but you are not giving evidence here. We'll verify it. Madam Registrar, the two pages extract from this testimony, what number is reserved for that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be P7414.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Reserved for that extract. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution quickly go to P4525.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm showing you this document because of what your view is concerning the precision of these air bombs, modified with rockets being attached with stabilisers. This document states -- it's a document from Pretis in Vogosca to the Main Staff rear command post dated 18 January, 1995. It states: "We kindly ask you to provide us with 600 pieces of FAB-250," which are 250 kilogramme air bombs. And then it says, "without a stabiliser, with fuses, for the completion of rocket motors, 122 millimetres with aerial bombs. FAB-250." "'Pretis' Holding Vogosca will manufacture all other positions for the rocket bombs." Sir, in addition to this the Chamber has also seen the rocket motors that have impacted in Sarajevo, some of which did have stabilisers, some which did not or had ones which did not open. I put it to you that there was no consistent practice of putting stabilisers on these motors. And, in fact, there were ones that were produced without any stabilisers. That's what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. And it says here that Pretis would make the other elements. I don't know whether they manufactured stabilisers or not, but they didn't really need what they made themselves because it says here that the other positions, I mean, they would regulate that. They will manufacture all other positions for the rocket bombs. That's what it says. So I guess it's not what they do, but I don't know that anybody targeted without stabilisers. So it could happen that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear what could happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But this possibility is not ruled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat the end of your answer about what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I got the impression that what then follows in the transcript is the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If that's the case, I wasn't sure it was complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at least that seems to be logical. Mr. Stojanovic is following in the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Part of what the witness said is missing. We could not hear it due to background noise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you said: "... it could happen that ..." Could you then repeat what you then said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could happen that when an air bomb is launched the stabiliser would not open and that then it would not take the right trajectory. That possibility exists with other artillery pieces too. There could be a technical error or something like that. I don't know if that happened but there is that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a few more questions that I would like to go through. Today, you had an opportunity to give answers - for the record, this is page 25, lines 16 to 25 of the transcript - what it means to implement fire or open fire in terms of artillery. So I would like to ask you what the term "implementing fire" means when it is in the order that you receive.

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all orders for combat activities that are issued by the superior command on the basis of which artillery orders are written up as well, what is noted is how the fire is planned, but it doesn't mean that this fire has to be open. However, if the order says "open fire," that means that this concrete order should be carried out, that a certain target should be engaged; whereas, implementing is the planning of this fire at some moment during combat operations. And as I said, several fires are planned. Now, which one will be opened or whether any one will be opened depends on the specific situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the basis of what does someone who is planning action and who is issuing an order for the use of artillery, on the basis of what does he state in his own document that fire should be implemented? On the basis of what does he envisage these places where fire may occur?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First there is planning of fire or rather it is order to implement fire against targets that have already been observed, and we have information exactly where these targets are. So the firing is planned with regard to these targets that have already been observed. Also, as the combat disposition moves during combat operations, then it is assumed where their next positions could be during withdrawal, and that is how fire is planned. In terms of such leaps. In terms of carrying out further tasks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P464, please. Could we have that document, now. This is a document that that we've had an opportunity to see already. It's a document of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. An order dated the 11th of October 1992. And I would like to ask that we move onto the next page in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where it says "Firing tasks." In the first line, it says: "Prevent the enemy's attack from Sarajevo aimed at lifting the blockade of Sarajevo by implementing [as read] fire at the areas of ..." And then the areas are listed here. These areas here, do they indicate to you why they are marked as firing tasks in this document?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because in these areas firing positions of the enemy artillery were observed. Larger calibres at that. And mortars, too, that fired at our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Stojanovic. You quoted this part and in the first line it says: "... attack from Sarajevo aimed at lifting the blockade ..." But I see it says open fire. "Prevent the enemy's attack from Sarajevo aimed at lifting the blockade of Sarajevo by opening fire ..." I don't know what it says in the B/C/S. But what you quoted to the witness says "by implementing fire at the earliest," and here it say I see "opening fire" in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the problem why we went back to this document, in the B/C/S version -- and that is why I asked my colleague to say that in English. In the B/C/S it clearly says "ostvariti."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ostvariti.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So it says "ostvariti," "implementing," not "opening," "otvarati"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try to deal with this as quickly as possible and I'll highlight that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, would you take a look at line 4 now. This is what it says: "Neutralise enemy artillery, implementing fire at the following areas ..." What about these areas? Do they indicate the reasons to you why this was included in the firing tasks that were given to you?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the areas are some of the ones that I mentioned in my statement as those where enemy artillery and mortars were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am going to complete the next paragraph. It says, I quote: "Neutralise enemy tanks by implementing fire at the area of Kosevsko Brdo." This area, Kosevsko Brdo, that an area where enemy tanks had been observed too?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And all the tasks that we mentioned earlier on are based on enemy firing positions that had already been established, of enemy artillery and mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have document P7402 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, this is a document that you had the opportunity to see yesterday. It's that table of signals and targets. Most of this document was shown to you. I would like to ask you to take a look at the next page as well and the next one, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for the next page in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what I'd like to ask you. Can you tell us on the basis of anything whether you could locate the time when this table of signals and targets was used?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at document P7408. First, let us look at the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You had the opportunity of seeing that. If you remember, this is a document dated the 14th of September, 1992. Commander Stanislav Galic. A document of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Could we please focus on paragraph 4 that has been put to you already. It's on the next page in B/C/S. And I would kindly ask that we move on to the next page in English as we start reading this. What it says here is as follows. "The Ilidza and Igman Brigades shall carry out in close co-ordination and agreement of the commanders an attack along the following axe: Doglodi-Bare axis toward Stupska Petlja and along the Otes-Stup interchange axis to unblock the village of Doglodi and save the Serbian population, and then continue operations to deblock and save the people and soldiers of Nedzarici." Please, could you tell us since precisely in this paragraph the 1st Sarajevo Brigade was mentioned and the support that the KAG is supposed to provide, what kind of blockade and what kind of saving of the Serb people is being referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the deblockade and saving of the Serb people from the area of Nedzarici. Throughout the war, they were in a terribly difficult position. They had only one street towards Ilidza. And they were suffering losses every day and they were being terrorised by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to conclude by using yet another document. You said several times, and you also said in your statement, you stated a fact that the UNPROFOR observers were at the locations that you marked today for my colleague, the Prosecutor. And these were the positions that were held by your unit. I would kindly ask you to tell us how this actually functions? You need to act on orders from your superior command. Is it your obligation to ask them for any kind of consent, or do you ask on the basis of the order issued by your superior command?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I acted on the orders issued by my superior officers, and UNPROFOR observers were right next to me. I mean, we were sitting in the same room, round-the-clock, 24 hours a day. We spent the night there, bed by bed. We were there together all the time. And whenever my brigade artillery fired, first of all he'd have to see that, hear that, and I would show it to him on the map. I would show the area, the co-ordinates of the target that I'm engaging, and he would see it himself. And I would tell me him which units I'm using and how many projectiles I'm using. He could see that, he could hear that because he was right there. So the period is June 1992 all the way up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see P7409 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You could already see this document before, Colonel, dated the 14th of September 1992. Let us look at paragraph 895 of this document. I believe it is on the third page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It is the second page in English. Paragraph 895.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the report, inter alia, it says as follows, perhaps you can follow me in the language you understand. "At Tilava, a mountainous area south of Sarajevo, at least a dozen 122 millimetre Serbian artillery guns were employed in the field. The Serbian Commander, Captain Savo Simic, was observed by three United Nations officials but fired one volley in what he said was a response to an attack by BiH Government forces in the suburb of Ilidza." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This kind of response or rather this kind of report of theirs, does it reflect what you just said in terms of how and in what way they could observe your work at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Another question for you. When they say he fired an artillery round --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is actually one volley.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent the translation is accurate, but what did they have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps they had a volley in mind of three projectiles. So it is possible that at least three projectiles were fired in the volley. That is probably that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I rise. I just noted one thing that the interpreters raised. There is a difference between the English original and the B/C/S translation as to whether it's a volley or round. In the B/C/S translation it says "one round," in the English original it says "one volley."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the best would indeed be to have the translation revised and not to read from the translation but rather from the original. Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Could you rephrase the question -- or as a matter of fact, I'll rephrase the question in English because you're a B/C/S speaker. Witness, you were asked earlier by Mr. Stojanovic: "When they say he fired an artillery volley ..." And could you resume from there what you wanted to ask the witness? Because you were interrupted there, Mr. Stojanovic. So the beginning of the question is: "When they say he fired an artillery volley ..." And could you now resume what you wanted to ask the witness, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quote the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "... and he said it was a response to an attack by BiH government forces in the suburb of Ilidza." Does this report of theirs accurately and precisely describe the process as it was observed by the observers through your interaction with them?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I do object to that characterisation of the document because what the document says is that that's what the witness said that it was, not, in fact, that that's what the observers were considering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But we have -- yes, you apparently agree, Mr. Stojanovic. It's what the document says is what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. I don't think that's in dispute. If I may be allowed another question and I can clear it up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Simic, let me conclude with this question: Can we see in the text that you informed them about the reasons why you approved for the volley to be used?

utterances.speaker: SAVO SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I informed them as is reflected in the report. I always did that. And they could note that themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weber, no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions from the Bench. Mr. Simic, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered the many questions that were put to you by the parties and by this Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest to the parties that we take a break -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of what the Chamber further has to do, we would like to take a break slightly longer than usual. We would resume then at quarter past 1.00, and it's our expectation that within, I would say, 35, 40 minutes after that we would be able to deliver the decisions that are on our list. Then finally, Mr. Stojanovic, I noticed that "opening fire" was now replaced by "implementing fire." And again, as a non-native speaking person, in trying to understand the language, I understand that "to implement" means either to carry out or to effect or to carry through or to complete or to apply or to perform or to realise or to fulfil or to execute or to discharge or to bring about or to put something into effect. To say that it's not yet entirely clear to me what the difference is with my understanding of "opening fire," that is firing, but I'm open for all submissions. I do not stick to any explanation, but apparently all these terms, "returning," "opening," "implementing," seem to need further interpretation. And to the extent the parties could assist the Chamber in that, me, as a nonspeaking speaker -- as a nonnative speaker, and perhaps some of my colleagues are as well, would appreciate such assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours if I may. I think it is a simple matter. We could just verify the word and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily to be done now immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But rather to think about it and to find a way how to best assist the Chamber in overcoming this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, on a related issue, you had asked about assistance that could be provided in terms of understanding how before an attack happens one could already know where to return fire upon. If you look at the transcript, page 26267, lines 19 through 26273, line 13, Witness Lucic there described how they had bands of fire 60 to 100 metres in front of the trenches where they would fire upon the enemy forces when they were attacking the trenches to defend the trenches. That may assist you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was clear to me. My problem was a slightly different one; that is, could you tell us two days in advance from where people would fire so that you could return that fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, there has been -- I think this witness and other witnesses have identified that artillery targets are all preselected and all premeasured so that they are in existence before, but I -- you know, I do understand, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, I heard that there were mobile mortars in Sarajevo, so -- and to already know from exactly what positions one would fire this axis. But I leave it open. It's still a matter for thoughts rather than for too much discussion at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could just try to clean up one housekeeping matter for the last witness so we can have a clean break. The 32641 has now be uploaded into e-court. This was the transcript excerpt that was referred to at the end of the examination that was assigned P07414. These are the official transcript pages and it is our understanding that Registry will then verify whether or not the transcript reflects the actual text. So we'd ask that that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: 65 ter 32641a be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, I think we had reserved a number for that. That was?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number was P7414.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And P7414, which is 65 ter 32641a, is admitted. We resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will deal with a few procedural matters. First the Chamber delivers a short statement on the reopening presentation of evidence. Yesterday, the Prosecution informed the Defence and the Chamber that it intended to file a bar table motion as part of the reopening of its case after its witnesses have given evidence. In its decision of the 23rd of October, 2014, the Chamber stated that it understood that the 60 documents the Prosecution intended to tender would be tendered in court through the witnesses. There was no intimation that the Prosecution would want to file a bar table motion in the litigation over the past year. Accordingly, the Chamber prefers to received the documentary evidence in court through the witnesses. Then I'll first deal with an oral decision on the expertise of Witness Milan Tutoric. On the 3rd of March, 2015, the Defence filed a motion to have Tutoric's statement admitted pursuant to Rules 92 per and 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. On the 2nd of April, the Prosecution submitted that while it does not challenge the expert status of Tutoric it does not accept the statement and requests to cross-examine him. The Prosecution further submits that it reserves its position to contest the relevance of the subject matter of the statement to the extent it challenges materials or findings that the Prosecution does not rely on. On a preliminary note, the Chamber recalls its 17th of March decision whereby it considered that the Defence is presenting Tutoric as a Rule 94 bis witness and not as a 92 ter witness. This can be found at transcript pages 33210 through 33211. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October 2012 decision concerning expert witness Richard Butler. The Chamber notes that the Defence has not specified Tutoric's field of expertise but gathers that it wishes to present him as an expert in qualitative and quantitative data analysis. The Chamber has reviewed Tutoric's curriculum vitae and statement which purports to provide a comparative analysis of lists of victims of the July 1995 Srebrenica events in order to establish whether he is a qualified expert in data analysis. However, the Chamber notes that Tutoric's education, as set out in his CV, does not establish that he is a qualified expert in this field. Furthermore, the CV does not refer to any publications or participation in any other scholarly activities in this presumed area of expertise. With regard to his work experience, the Chamber notes that Tutoric spent most of his career in law enforcement and security. Recently, he has been working at the Centre for Research on War, War Crimes, and the Search for Missing Persons since April 2012 as a project manager, although not as a researcher or a scientist. Furthermore, the Chamber reviewed Tutoric's statement to see if it demonstrates that he is an expert in the field. In this respect, the Chamber finds that the statement does not present a clear and methodologically sound data analysis as would be expected of an expert. The witness also introduces factual information in his statement but fails to cite references. Therefore, the Chamber finds that neither Tutoric's CV nor his statement demonstrate that Tutoric has the specialised knowledge required to testify as an expert witness and denies the Defence motion. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I now move to a decision on the admission of MFI D936. On the 16th of March of this year the Defence requested the admission into evidence of D936 as an exhibit associated with Milenko Karisik's witness statement. The Prosecution opposed admission and the Defence withdrew its tendering. On the 17th of March, after the Prosecution challenged paragraph 19 of the witness statement, the Defence re-tendered pages 5 through 11 of D936 and the Prosecution reiterated its opposition to admission as an associated exhibit. This can found at transcript pages 33123, -145, and 33253 to -256. Paragraph 19 of the witness statement refers to an agreement reached at the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 31st of March 1992, P3009, and it refers to the agreement to split up the BH MUP into Serbian and Bosnian parts. The witness stated that this division was in accordance with the so-called Lisbon treaty, also known as the Carrington Cutileiro plan. During cross-examination, the Prosecution questioned the witness's evidence that the agreement to split up the BH MUP was part of the Cutileiro plan. To rebut this challenge, the Defence re-tendered parts of D936, a transcript excerpt dated the 22nd of March 2011 of Alija Delimustafic, his testimony, in the case against Momcilo Mandic before a court in Bosnia. In it, Delimustafic shared some light in the decision-making process in the collegium of the BH MUP, a body he states was composed of Serb, Croat, and Muslim representatives. The Chamber recalls its guidance of the 11th of December 2012 where it stated in instances in which an associated exhibit mainly corroborates the evidence of a witness, there may be no need to tender it, though such tendering may become necessary under Rule 89(C) upon a challenge to the witness's evidence if the exhibit has the potential to counter that challenge. The Chamber understands the Defence's retendering of parts D936 to fall within this category as both parties agreed that the document was not indispensable for understanding paragraph 19 of the witness statement. The Chamber considers the exhibit to have sufficient relevance and probative value for admission, because although Delimustafic could not recall whether the collegium had been involved in the decision to separate and relocate BH special police units along ethnic lines, it explains the witness's evidence regarding the collectively decision-making process in the collegium of the BH MUP at the time which had been challenged by the Prosecution. For these reasons, the Chamber admits into evidence page 5 up to and including page 11 of D936 in order to properly assess the context of pages 5 through 11, the Chamber will also admit the first two pages of the document into evidence. The Defence is instructed to upload these excerpts into e-court. The Chamber instructs the Registry to replace the existing Exhibit D936 with these new excerpts. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on this matter. I now move on to a decision on the expertise of Witness Milos Kovic. A decision with regard to his analysis of Prosecution expert reports authored by Witness Robert Donia and Patrick Treanor. On the 30th of March of 2015, the Defence filed a notice of disclosure of Milos Kovic's expert report pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecution filed its notice pursuant to the same rule on 24th of April, submitting that while it does not challenge the expert status of Kovic or the relevance of his reports, it does not accept the conclusions of his reports and therefore wishes to cross-examine him. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October 2012 decision concerning expert witness, Richard Butler. On the basis of Kovic's curriculum vitae and considering that the Prosecution does not dispute Kovic's qualification as an expert in the field of political history, the Chamber is satisfied that he has the specialised knowledge and expertise and that such knowledge and expertise may be of assistance to the Chamber in assessing the expert evidence presented by the Prosecution during its case in chief. With regard to the Prosecution's request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the Defence plans to call Kovic to give evidence. The Prosecution will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine him. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, that Kovic may be called to testify as an expert witness and shall be made available for cross-examination by the Prosecution. The Chamber defers its decision on the admission of the reports to the time of his testimony. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The Chamber will now deliver its decision on the expertise of Mile Dosenovic with regard to his report entitled "Communications in the Army of Republika Srpska with special emphasis on interception." On the 10th of April 2015, the Defence filed a notice of disclosure of Mile Dosenovic's expert report pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Prosecution filed its notice pursuant to Rule 94 bis on the 30th of April submitting that while it does not challenge the expert status of Dosenovic or the relevance of his report, it does not accept the conclusions of the report and therefore wishes to cross-examine him. On the 12th of May, the Defence filed a response to the Prosecution's 30th April submission. On the 19th of May, the Prosecution sought leave to reply and filed its reply to the Defence response. The Chamber will address the 12th and 19th of May submissions in a separate decision. With respect to the applicable law concerning expert evidence, the Chamber recalls and refers to its 19th of October 2012 decision concerning Richard Butler. On the basis of Dosenovic's curriculum vitae and considering that the Prosecution does not dispute Dosenovic's qualification as a military communication expert, the Chamber is satisfied that he has specialised knowledge and expertise and that such knowledge and expertise may be of assistance to the Chamber in understanding the communication systems used by the VRS. With regard to the Prosecution's request to cross-examine the witness, the Chamber notes that the Defence plans to call Dosenovic to give evidence. The Prosecution will therefore have the opportunity to cross-examine him. Based on the foregoing, the Chamber decides pursuant to Rule 94 bis of the Rules that the Defence may call Mile Dosenovic to testify as an expert witness and that he shall be made available for cross-examination by the Prosecution. The Chamber defers its decision on the admission of Mile Dosenovic's expert report to the time of his testimony. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. I move to the next decision. The decision the Chamber delivers is the decision on the remaining associated exhibits tendered through Witness Milomir Savcic. On the 29th of January, 2015, the Defence filed tendering the written statement of Milomir Savcic together with 14 associated exhibits. In its response of the 12th of February, the Prosecution did not oppose the motion. During the testimony of Savcic on the 25th of March, the Chamber admitted into evidence his written statement as Exhibit D968 and four exhibits, which had been listed as associated exhibits by the Defence in its 92 ter motion but eventually were tendered into evidence by the Prosecution during cross-examination admitted as P7266 up to and including P7269. The same day, the Defence stated that it withdraws the tendering of two other documents. The Chamber reserved exhibit numbers D969 up to and including D975 for the remaining documents. This can be found at transcript pages 33639 and -640. The Chamber recalls that the case law with regard to the admission of associated exhibits establishes that documents can be admitted if they form an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's written testimony. In order to satisfy this test, the witness's statement would have to be incomprehensible or at least of less probative value without the admission into evidence of the associated exhibits in question. The Chamber finds that the statement of Milomir Savcic is fully comprehensible without associated exhibits D969, D970, D971, and D972, and D973 because these documents include no additional information than what is already given by the witness in paragraphs 75, 84, 44, 38, and 45, respectively, of his statement. The Chamber further finds that without the additional information in Exhibits D974 and D975, the witness's statement would be incomprehensible and therefore the Chamber finds that these exhibits form an inseparable and indispensable part of the statement. The Chamber therefore admits D974 and D975 into evidence as associated exhibits to Milomir Savcic's statement and denies the admission of documents D969 up until and including D973. And this concludes the Chamber's decision. The Chamber now delivers its decision on the Defence request on the 12th of December, 2014, to add 17 documents to its Rule 65 ter list and have these documents admitted as associated exhibits to Goran Krcmar's witness statement admitted as D916. On the 19th of December the Prosecution filed its response, not taking a position on these requests. Dealing first with a request to add documents to the Defence's exhibit list, the Chamber recalls the case law with regard to amendments to exhibit lists which provides that a Chamber may, in the exercise of its inherent discretion in managing the trial proceedings, authorise requested additions to the exhibit list if it is satisfied that it is in the interests of justice to do so. The Defence submits that it only finalised Krcmar's statement after filing its exhibit list and therefore it could not have included the 17 documents. While the Chamber does not consider that this amounts to a showing of good cause, it does consider that the documents are prima facie probative and relevant to the indictment. Furthermore, the Prosecution did not raise any objections. Accordingly, the Chamber finds it to be in the interest of justice to allow the addition of the 17 documents to the Defence's exhibit list. Moving to the Defence request to admit the 17 documents as associated exhibits to D916, the Chamber recalls that documents can be admitted if they form an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's written testimony. In order to satisfy this test, the tendering party must demonstrate that the witness's evidence would be incomprehensible or of less probative value without the admission of the relevant associated exhibits into evidence. The Chamber has discussed its interpretation of this case law at transcript pages 530 to 531 and 5601 to 5603, and in its written decisions of the 23rd of July 2012 and the 7th of February 2013. Having moved the test, the Chamber finds that the requested documents form an inseparable and indispensable part of the witness's written testimony as, without their admission, Witness Krcmar's evidence would be incomprehensible or of less probative value. The Chamber hereby admits documents bearing Rule 65 ter numbers 1D05235 through 1D05243 and 1D05245 through 1D05249 into evidence as associated exhibits to the written statement of Witness Krcmar. The Chamber notes that the Defence is awaiting CLSS translations for documents bearing 65 ter numbers 1D05233, 1D05234, and 1D05244. Therefore, the Chamber marks these documents for identification pending translations. The Registrar is requested to assign exhibit numbers and MFI numbers by way of filing an internal memorandum. And this conclude's the Chamber's decision. The last decision should be delivered in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. If any of the decisions delivered by the Chamber triggers the need to address the Chamber and before the four non-sitting weeks which are before us, then a brief opportunity will be given to any party that feels the need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Mr. President, actually not related to any of the decisions the Chamber has just read, but the Chamber will have seen, as did we, the Defence this morning filed the Rule 92 ter motion for Witness Zdravko Salipur. We note that he's on the July schedule that the Defence circulated yesterday. He's also one of the subjects of the Defence's motion to add a number of witnesses. He's one of the ones the Prosecution had not objected to, and we wouldn't -- the Defence has informally communicated to us that they would appreciate that the same approach be taken as with Witness Simic, that the addition be informally granted or be formally granted, reasons to follow. We would have no objection to that approach if the Chamber is also agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be adding it to the 65 ter list? That is the issue at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I'd invite my colleagues to correct me if I've erred at all in setting out our understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi has been rather precise and accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We had not seen it yet but adding to the 65 ter list is a decision which is -- well, has not a final impact on the case as a whole, and it's rather a decision which is not purely administrative but to some extent is. I'll just consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber rules on the request and allows the Defence to add Witness Zdravko Salipur to its 65 ter witness list. One issue. Is it on the July list we -- is scheduled for July?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes. And I think the Defence circulated, again I'd invite them, I think they circulated it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is also accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And when in July?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The copy my colleague is showing me says the end of the first of the two sitting weeks that they and we anticipate would follow the presentation of reopening evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there is any time left after that, then -- so these are -- that would be just briefly before the summer recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone seems to be in agreement. We -- Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know whether you are moving on to something else, but before we adjourned I wanted to take the opportunity presented by the Court to address any additional matters. Not necessarily specifically related to the matters discussed in Court thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. If it's an urgent matter, we'll certainly now listen to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There will always be a may to communicate with the Court. We are not in recess, even if we might not all be in The Hague --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can, I was just reminded. If we can move into private session quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Nothing else on the agenda. We'll adjourn for a longer period than usual, still a lot of work to be done before we resume, and that will be on the 22nd of June of this year, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
